Internal engineering memo: buy more local AI hardware, or use what we already own better?

Recommendation up front: do not commit to a broad hardware expansion this cycle. Fund a utilisation and reliability program first, with a narrow, reversible pilot for specific bottlenecks. Revisit capital purchases after we have four to six weeks of clean telemetry and a clear list of workloads that cannot be served well by the current estate.

The temptation to buy is understandable. Local inference is attractive because it keeps data inside our boundary, avoids per-token external pricing, and gives us more control over latency and failure modes. But “we need more GPUs” is not yet a technical conclusion. It is a symptom. The first question is whether the hardware we own is being used in a way that matches the workloads we actually run.

Cost is the easiest dimension to misread. A new server has a sticker price, but the real cost includes power, cooling, rack space, maintenance, spare parts, staff time, and the opportunity cost of capital that could instead fund evaluation, observability, or product work. If utilization is low, buying more hardware multiplies the fixed cost without improving throughput. If utilization is high but latency is poor, the problem may be scheduling, batching, model choice, quantization, or network path rather than raw silicon. Either way, the purchase decision should follow evidence, not enthusiasm.

Latency deserves separate treatment. Some workloads are interactive and sensitive to tail latency; others are batch jobs where throughput matters more than a few extra milliseconds. We should not force one policy across both. Interactive paths need tight queues, admission control, and predictable fallback behavior. Batch paths can tolerate queuing if they improve utilization. A memo that says “more hardware” without separating these cases will produce the wrong purchase.

Reliability is where local hardware can either shine or disappoint. Owning the stack gives us control over upgrades, but it also concentrates risk: driver regressions, thermal events, power interruptions, storage contention, and operator error all become our problem. External services offer managed resilience, but they introduce dependency, data-flow constraints, and variable pricing. The right answer is likely hybrid: keep sensitive or latency-critical workloads local, but design them with the same operational discipline as production services. That means health checks, load shedding, canary deployments, rollback plans, and clear ownership.

Opportunity cost is easy to understate. Every dollar spent on accelerators is a dollar not spent on evaluation harnesses, model selection, prompt and retrieval quality, or developer tooling. If our current models are too large for the task, the cheapest improvement may be a smaller model, a better retrieval index, or a tighter output contract. If our current models are too small, the issue is capability, not capacity. We need to know which one we have.

Reversibility favors the cautious path. A software and scheduling change can be rolled back in minutes. A hardware purchase is harder to unwind and may strand capacity if the workload mix shifts. A pilot is therefore the right middle ground: buy or rent a small amount of additional capacity only for a named workload, with a time-boxed success criterion, and a pre-agreed exit if it does not help.

Uncertainty is real. We do not yet have enough data to know whether the bottleneck is compute, memory bandwidth, storage, network, or model choice. We also do not know how demand will change next quarter. That is exactly why the first step should be measurement rather than procurement.

Concretely, I propose the following. Instrument utilization, queue depth, p50 and p95 latency, failure rate, and cost per useful request for the next four to six weeks. Segment workloads by interactive and batch. Review whether any local models can be replaced by smaller or more efficient variants. Then ask a narrow question: which workloads, if any, cannot meet latency or reliability targets with the current estate? Only those should enter a pilot.

My recommendation is therefore: improve utilization first, defer broad hardware expansion, and authorize a limited pilot for proven bottlenecks. If the pilot shows that the current estate is structurally insufficient, then a larger purchase becomes justified. If it shows that the estate is merely poorly scheduled, the savings will be larger and faster than any new purchase. Either way, we should avoid buying capacity before we understand the shape of the problem.

Internal engineering memo: local AI hardware versus better utilisation

To: platform and ML engineering leads
From: infrastructure review
Re: whether to buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of what we own

Recommendation up front: do not make a large hardware purchase yet. Run a focused utilisation and latency programme for the next two quarters, instrument the workloads, and buy only the capacity that remains demonstrably short after scheduling, batching, caching, quantization, and routing improvements. If the gap persists, purchase a modest, reversible expansion rather than a fleet-wide refresh.

The case for buying more hardware is understandable. Local inference avoids some external dependency, can keep sensitive prompts and data inside our boundary, and may reduce per-request latency when traffic is predictable. It also gives the team a sense of control. But those benefits are easy to overstate. Hardware is a blunt instrument: it adds throughput only if the software can use it, and it adds fixed cost whether the workload is busy or idle. A GPU that sits at 18 percent utilisation for most of the day is not a capacity asset; it is a recurring liability with a fan.

The case for improving utilisation is stronger today. Our current estate appears to be fragmented across a few nodes, with ad hoc deployments, inconsistent batching, and limited visibility into queue depth, tail latency, memory pressure, and model residency. That pattern wastes money in several ways. Small requests are sent to large models when a distilled or quantized model would meet the quality bar. Idle models remain loaded in memory while other requests wait. Retries and duplicate evaluations inflate load. Scheduling is optimistic, so bursts arrive faster than the system can drain. These are engineering problems, not physics problems.

Cost should be evaluated over total cost of ownership, not sticker price. Purchased hardware carries depreciation, power, cooling, maintenance, spare parts, staff time, and the risk of obsolescence. Leased or rented capacity shifts some of that risk but can reintroduce external dependency and variable pricing. Utilisation improvements reduce the need for both. If we raise average utilisation from, say, 20 to 50 percent without degrading p95 latency, we may defer a purchase by a full cycle. That is not a guarantee, but it is a plausible and testable outcome.

Latency deserves separate treatment. Local hardware can help when requests are frequent, local, and latency-sensitive, especially for interactive features where network jitter matters. But latency is not determined by the accelerator alone. It is determined by queueing, model size, batching policy, cache hit rate, and whether the right model is chosen for the task. A larger GPU with poor scheduling can be slower than a smaller one with disciplined routing. We should measure p50, p95, and p99 by workload class, not only average throughput.

Reliability is also central. More hardware can improve resilience if it is used to isolate critical services and remove single points of failure. But more hardware can also increase failure surface: more drivers, more nodes, more configuration drift, more firmware updates, and more operational states. The safer path is to make the existing estate observable and boring: health checks, automatic failover, capacity headroom, and clear ownership. If a model is critical, replicate it. If it is not, do not pay for redundancy we do not need.

Opportunity cost matters. Every dollar spent on hardware is a dollar not spent on evaluation, data quality, observability, or product features. A small team cannot absorb a large capital commitment and also keep pace with model changes. Buying too early can also lock us into a stack that becomes stale as inference techniques improve. Buying too late can leave users waiting and force emergency purchases at worse prices. The right answer is staged.

Reversibility favours the utilisation-first path. Software changes are easier to undo than a rack of accelerators. We can roll back a scheduler, adjust a cache, or change a routing policy. We cannot easily unwind a purchase, especially if the hardware is committed to a long-term contract. That asymmetry should guide the decision.

Uncertainty remains. We do not yet know the true demand curve, the quality sensitivity of each workload, or how much latency is caused by software versus hardware. The plan should therefore include a short experiment: instrument the system, classify workloads, test batching and routing, and review results after a defined period. If p95 latency and utilisation improve, defer the purchase. If not, and the shortfall is stable, buy a limited expansion with a clear exit or lease option.

Bottom line: improve utilisation first, buy only for proven shortfall, and keep the purchase small and reversible. This is not a claim that hardware is unimportant. It is a claim that the next dollar is more likely to buy value in the software and operating model than in another box.

appliance.competing_traffic: none (the voice engines suspended through LLooM for the window)
appliance.drafter: DFlash2 (incoai/Inkling-2-Mini-DFlash2 @ 4f9088ea66c2), greedy drafts: 7 draft tokens with one live request, 3 each with two, plain decode from three (ATLAS_DFLASH_BATCH_DEPTH=1:7,2:3,1000000:0); verifies stop where the drafter is unsure (ATLAS_DFLASH_CONF_WIDTH=1: the engine learns while serving how often each draft confidence is accepted), drafts go off for a sequence whose steps stop paying, for 32 tokens at first and doubling while re-probes fail (ATLAS_DFLASH_ADAPTIVE=1, threshold 1.0 (ATLAS_DFLASH_ADAPTIVE_MIN=1.0) accepted a block), in place of the engine throughput gate (ATLAS_MTP_GATE_FORCE=1)
appliance.kv_cache_dtype: auto (bf16), window-bounded: the 40 sliding-window visits keep their last 1,024 tokens
appliance.quantisation: TML modelopt as shipped: NVFP4 experts L0-19, MXFP8 experts L20-23, BF16 rest; prefill quantizes the checkpoint experts' inputs as its hf_quant_config.json requires (NVFP4 / MXFP8 rows, W4A4 / W8A8)
appliance.scheduler: SparkInkling default profile: max-num-seqs 8, gpu-memory-utilization 0.80, prefill chunks 4096, CUDA graphs, programmatic dependent launch (ATLAS_INKLING2_PDL=1), prefix caching with conv-state snapshots (--enable-prefix-caching, --ssm-cache-slots=264, ATLAS_QWEN4EXP_AUX_PINNED=1) and branch checkpoints (ATLAS_GLM_PC_BRANCH=1, ATLAS_GLM_PC_BRANCH_MIN=512), --request-timeout=3600, --tool-max-tokens=32768
